title: Disagreeing well
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: haud sciō an MEANS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE, and it is the politest disagreement in the language. Word for word it is 'I do not know whether it is true'; as an idiom it is 'I rather think it IS true'. The understatement is so settled that it reversed — so an English speaker reads doubt where a Roman heard gentle assertion. L2-M5's benignē was the same kind of trap, and like benignē it has to be learned as a phrase or not used at all.

nesciō an IS THE GENUINE DOUBT AND haud sciō an IS NOT, which is the module's central pair: one word apart and opposite in force. And the idiom takes haud, never nōn — haud denies a single WORD rather than a clause, and nōn sciō an is a plain statement of ignorance, which is what the words say and not what the phrase means. One wrong negative and the understatement is gone.

nesciō IS THE FIFTH WORD IN THIS COURSE WITH A NEGATIVE INSIDE IT, after L1-M3's nōlō, L2-M9's mālō, L3-M5's negō and M3's nisi. By now that is a habit of the language rather than a list of exceptions, and it is worth naming as one: Latin prefers to weld a negative into a word than to put one beside it.

nōn omnīnō GIVES YOU THE MIDDLE GROUND L3-M3's cōnsentiō DID NOT HAVE. That module's agreement was all or nothing; nōn omnīnō cōnsentiō qualifies instead of refusing. And the ORDER is load-bearing: nōn omnīnō is 'not entirely' and omnīnō nōn is 'entirely not', which is stronger than a flat refusal. Both are grammatical, which is what makes the position matter.

THE POTENTIAL SUBJUNCTIVE IS THE MODULE'S ONE NEW USE OF A MOOD IT ALREADY HAS. L3-M4 opened the present subjunctive for conditions, purpose and advice; here the same forms say 'might' standing alone — dīcat aliquis, 'someone might say'; fortasse vērum sit, 'it might perhaps be true'. No new endings, one new job. L3-M3 wrote fortasse with a plain indicative and said it changed nothing else; with the mood it gives a second degree of hedge.

THE REPORTED CLAUSE IS L3-M3's AND L3-M5's, UNCHANGED: dīcat aliquis mē errāvisse. mē rather than sē, because the person reported is the speaker — which was L3-M10's last mistake plate — and a perfect infinitive because the wrongness is earlier than the saying.

velim PLUS A SUBJUNCTIVE IS A WISH ABOUT SOMEBODY ELSE, and it needs no ut at all: velim cōnsentiās, 'I should like you to agree'. L2-M1 wrote velim with a plain object for twenty-five modules and M3 showed it was a present subjunctive all along — this is the fuller construction, and the absent ut is the one thing about it an English speaker will not expect.

A NEUTER ADJECTIVE BECOMES A NOUN BY BEING USED AS ONE: vērum is 'true' in haud sciō an vērum sit and 'the truth' in an vērum dīxerīs, and nothing about the word changes. Latin does this freely and English does it with a handful of words like 'the good'. L3-M3's vērō was the same word's ablative doing an adverb's job, which makes three uses of one stem across two levels.

tamen COMES SECOND IN ITS CLAUSE EVEN WHEN THAT CUTS AN IDIOM IN HALF: haud tamen sciō an vērum sit. Six words in this course must come second and there is no exception for a fixed phrase — which is the module's hardest positional fact, because splitting haud sciō an feels like breaking it and is what the rule requires.

words.note: 'He might say' — the POTENTIAL subjunctive. Same shape L3-M4 opened for purpose and conditions, saying 'might' on its own; putet is putō in the same mood.
'Someone, anyone' — aliquis as a subject. It is quis with ali- in front, so the question word has become an indefinite.
'Me' — the accusative of a reported clause, and it is mē rather than sē because the person reported is the speaker. L3-M10's last plate was this.
'To have gone wrong' — the perfect infinitive of errō. M3's shape, inside L3-M3's construction.

words.note: 'Not' — but it denies a single WORD rather than a clause, and it is the negative this idiom takes. nōn is the ordinary one and will not do here.

sentences.trap: The hedge and the concession together, and the hedge is doing the work of an admission. haud sciō an errāverim is as close as this language gets to 'I think I may have been wrong' — and because the idiom asserts rather than doubts, it is an admission in the shape of a doubt.

sentences.display: Licet errāverim, haud sciō an tū quoque errāveris.
sentences.cue: Although I may have been wrong, I rather think you were wrong too.
sentences.literal: granted I-may-have-erred not I-know whether you also you-may-have-erred

words.note: 'Although, granted that' — and it takes a subjunctive. M4's word.
'That I may have gone wrong' — the perfect subjunctive of errō.
'Not' — but it denies a single WORD rather than a clause, and it is the negative this idiom takes. nōn is the ordinary one and will not do here.
'I know': sciō 'I know', scit 'he knows', nesciō 'I do not know'. English 'science' and 'conscious' come from it.
'Whether', with a subjunctive after it.
'You', one person — and it is here for the contrast, which is the one job a pronoun has. L1-M2's row.
'Also', and it comes SECOND in its clause. L1-M10's word.
'That you may have gone wrong' — the perfect subjunctive of errō in the you-shape.

sentences.trap: Concede, then turn it round, and both halves are in the same mood for different reasons: licet demands a subjunctive and an demands one too. So the sentence has four subjunctive shapes in it and only one of them is a hedge — the others are what their conjunctions require.
